note: SOURCE for the Class B (derived-from-spec-algorithm) conformance vectors — the map/set cases whose CANONICAL ENTRY/ELEMENT ORDER is defined by ontos-codec-v1 byte order (ontos-codec.md §6 / ontos-data.md §5.7–§5.8) and is therefore impractical to hand-compute. This file is the HUMAN-AUTHORED ORACLE: a maintainer authors the INTENT — the membership of each map/set — in a DELIBERATELY NON-CANONICAL (reverse) order, plus an `order_explanation` stating why the canonical order is what it is, by codec bytes. The generator tools/vector/gen.mjs derives the sorted `value` + `hex` (via @bitspark/ontos-data's encodeMap/encodeSet, which SORT, then @bitspark/ontos-codec's encode) into vectors/data.generated.json, and ASSERTS that each derived {value,hex} reproduces the corresponding case already pinned in vectors/data.json byte-for-byte (which is itself pinned to all four encoders by the codec vector-runner). The committed generated bytes are a REVIEWED ARTIFACT, not the oracle itself: the oracle is THIS source plus the specified derivation rule. See docs/conformance-vector-provenance.md. Authoring notation: a value is { "atom": "<lowercase-hex>" } or { "tuple": [ <value>, … ] } (vectors/README.md). Atom-byte labels: int=696e74, bool=626f6f6c, utf8-text=757466382d74657874, map=6d6170, set=736574. The codec encodes Atom(b)=00‖uvarint(len)‖b and Tuple(v*)=01‖uvarint(arity)‖encode(child)*, so order(A,B)=lexicographic(encode A, encode B): a bare atom (tag 00) always sorts before any tuple/embedding (tag 01); among atoms, shorter-or-lexicographically-smaller bytes sort first; among embeddings, the comparison runs over the full encoding (label bytes then payload). For each entry below, `provenance` is "derived-from-spec-algorithm"; `entries` (map) is an array of [key,value] pairs and `elements` (set) is an array of values, each given in REVERSE of the canonical codec order so that the human authors membership without pre-sorting and the generator is what produces the sorted bytes.

cases.name: map_empty
cases.order_explanation: Zero entries: the empty map is Tuple(Atom("map")) (label bytes 6d6170, arity 1). The strict-ascending invariant holds vacuously; nothing to order.

cases.name: map_one_int_text
cases.order_explanation: One entry, key int 1 → value utf8-text "hi". A single key needs no ordering; it is well-formed because there is no adjacent pair to compare.

cases.name: map_two_atom_keys
cases.order_explanation: Authored reversed (0x62 before 0x61). Canonical order is 0x61 then 0x62: encode(Atom(0x61))=000161 and encode(Atom(0x62))=000162 share tag 00 and length 01 and differ at the last byte 61<62, so 0x61 sorts first.

cases.name: map_mixed_keys
cases.order_explanation: Authored reversed (utf8-text "a", int 1, atom 0x61). Canonical order is by codec bytes, NOT by kind: bare-atom key 0x61 (encode=000161, tag 00) sorts before BOTH embedding keys (tag 01); between the two embeddings int 1 (encode=01020003696e7400020001) and utf8-text "a" (encode=01020009757466382d74657874000161) the label-length uvarint differs first — 03 < 09 — so int 1 precedes utf8-text "a". Final order: 0x61, int 1, "a".

cases.name: map_prefix_keys
cases.order_explanation: Authored reversed (0x6161 before 0x61). Canonical order is 0x61 then 0x6161: encode(Atom(0x61))=000161 and encode(Atom(0x6161))=00026161 share tag 00 but the length uvarint differs — 01 < 02 — so the shorter-payload key 0x61 sorts first. (The codec is length-prefixed, so 0x61 is NOT a byte-prefix of 0x6161's encoding; their lengths decide the order.)

cases.name: map_nested_value
cases.order_explanation: One entry, key atom 0x6b → value the empty map Tuple(Atom("map")). A single key needs no ordering; the nested map value is carried verbatim (no recursion into value canonicality).

cases.name: map_map_key
cases.order_explanation: One entry whose KEY is itself a map {0x61: int 1} (an arbitrary L0 value is a valid key, with a unique encoding hence a definite sort position) → value bool true. A single key needs no ordering.

cases.name: map_noncanonical_int_key
cases.datum: { int(000001): 0x00 } (non-canonical int key, accepted — no recursion)
cases.order_explanation: One entry whose key is shaped like an int but has a non-minimal magnitude (000001). map well-formedness is structural + codec-order only and does NOT recurse into key canonicality, so this is an accepted key (a valid L0 value with a unique encoding); it is simply not also a recognized int. A single key needs no ordering.

cases.name: set_empty
cases.order_explanation: Zero elements: the empty set is Tuple(Atom("set")) (label bytes 736574, arity 1). The strict-ascending invariant holds vacuously; nothing to order.

cases.name: set_one_int
cases.order_explanation: One element, int 1. A single element needs no ordering.

cases.name: set_two_atoms
cases.order_explanation: Authored reversed (0x62 before 0x61). Canonical order is 0x61 then 0x62: encode(Atom(0x61))=000161 and encode(Atom(0x62))=000162 differ only at the final byte 61<62, so 0x61 sorts first.

cases.name: set_mixed
cases.order_explanation: Authored reversed (utf8-text "a", int 1, atom 0x61). Canonical order is by codec bytes, NOT by kind: bare-atom element 0x61 (encode=000161, tag 00) sorts before BOTH embeddings (tag 01); between int 1 (encode=01020003696e7400020001) and utf8-text "a" (encode=01020009757466382d74657874000161) the label-length uvarint differs first — 03 < 09 — so int 1 precedes "a". Final order: 0x61, int 1, "a".

cases.name: set_nested
cases.order_explanation: Authored reversed ({0x61} before {}). Canonical order is the empty set {} then {0x61}: encode(Tuple(Atom("set")))=01010003736574 and encode(Tuple(Atom("set"),Atom(0x61)))=01020003736574000161 share tag 01 but the arity uvarint differs — 01 < 02 — so the empty set sorts first.

cases.name: set_noncanonical_int_elem
cases.datum: { int(000001) } (non-canonical int element, accepted — no recursion)
cases.order_explanation: One element shaped like an int but with a non-minimal magnitude (000001). set well-formedness is structural + codec-order only and does NOT recurse into element canonicality, so this is an accepted element; it is simply not also a recognized int. A single element needs no ordering.
